title: Languages of the court
hook: he wrote in Braj, Persian and Punjabi

segments.voice: Yesterday, names of weapons: a garland of blades used to name the power that protects. Your line was tools for good. Which tool did you put to work? Day one thousand two hundred forty.

Over the last two weeks, the readings have quietly changed language under our feet. The letter to the emperor: Persian. The war ballad whose first lines open the Ardas: Punjabi. The swayyas, the praise of the Khalsa, the garland of weapon names: mostly Braj, a literary language of poets in northern India. Three languages, one writer. That's not an accident of translation. Readers see a choice in it, a tongue for each job, and today is about why that matters.
screen: `THE LETTER: PERSIAN.` → `THE BALLAD: PUNJABI.` → `THE POEMS: MOSTLY BRAJ.`

segments.voice: Each language is a door into a different room. Persian was the language of the Mughal court, of government and letters between powers. So the letter to the emperor went in Persian verse, the court's own literary language, the language its reader worked in every day. Punjabi was the language of the people at home, of the fields and villages. A var, a ballad of courage, belongs there, so Chandi di Var is in Punjabi, the tongue its listeners breathed in. Braj was the language of poetry across a wide stretch of northern India, the one poets used for devotion and for story. Much of the Guru's longer poetry is in Braj, written in the Gurmukhi script. There's something deeper, too. Jaap Sahib, one of the Sikh morning prayers, is full of names for God, and some readers notice that it draws them from more than one world. Alongside names rooted in Sanskrit, it calls God Razak, the provider, and Rahim, the merciful, words that come from Arabic and Persian. It's the move Akal Ustat and the Zafarnama's opening made, carried into a daily prayer. One God, praised in the vocabularies of neighbors who often didn't share a prayer. For Sikhs that fits a long thread. The Guru Granth Sahib itself gathers voices from many regions and backgrounds. Many tongues, one Name. Language, in this tradition, isn't a fence around the holy. It's a set of doors, and the Guru walked through several of them.
screen: `PERSIAN: THE LANGUAGE OF THE COURT.` · `PUNJABI: THE LANGUAGE OF HOME.` · `BRAJ: THE LANGUAGE OF POETS.` · `ONE GOD, MANY VOCABULARIES.` · then, large: `MANY TONGUES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a word in another language. Settle, and breathe. Pick a word you know in a language that isn't your first: thank you, peace, hello, mother, God, water. It doesn't matter how well you speak it. Say it once, quietly, and notice how it sits in your mouth. Then bring to mind the people who say that word every day without thinking. Let them be near for a breath or two. If you pray, you can follow the word with Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Languages of the court. Guru Gobind Singh wrote in Persian for the emperor, Punjabi for the people, and Braj for poetry. Today's word.
Your line: many tongues. Today, learn the word for thank you in the first language of someone you see often, and use it with them. Day one thousand two hundred forty.

howItsDone: Sikhs recite Guru Gobind Singh's compositions in their original languages, Braj, Persian and Punjabi, usually printed in Gurmukhi script, and teachers explain them in katha in Punjabi, English and other languages.

notes: Language assignments (Zafarnama Persian; Chandi di Var Punjabi; Akal Ustat, 33 Swayye, Khalsa Mahima, Shastar Nam Mala 'mostly Braj') are general descriptions; please confirm, especially Khalsa Mahima and Shastar Nam Mala as Braj.
Persian as the language of the Mughal court and Braj as a literary language of northern Indian poetry are general history notes, not taken from a cited text; please confirm the wording.
